title: How to hire a design and development studio
metaTitle: How to hire a design studio
excerpt: Hire a studio whose portfolio matches the work, whose own people will do it, and who will leave you owning the repository, the domain, and the content.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The room is the kind of working session you are hiring, not a slide about it.
caption: Hire the people who will be in the room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should I look for in a studio portfolio?
faqs.answer: Look for the kind of work you need: a marketing site, a brand shop, or a product interface. Read whether the studio names the constraint and the decision, and whether it built the result. A gallery of screenshots without a decision is decoration.

faqs.question: Who should do the work after I hire?
faqs.answer: Ask who will design and who will write the production code, and whether those people are in the studio. A sales presentation followed by a handoff to an unnamed team is a different engagement. You are hiring the practice, not the pitch.

faqs.question: What should I own when the project ends?
faqs.answer: Own the repository, the domain, the analytics, and the content logins. Brand files should live somewhere you can open after launch. A studio that keeps those is a dependency. A studio that hands them over is a partner.

markdown:
Hire a design studio for three things you can check: the portfolio contains the kind of work you need, the people who will do it are the people you can meet, and you will own the result when the project ends.

A studio is a fit when design and production code come from the same small team, for a launch you can describe. It is a poor fit when you need a single afternoon of help, or a permanent department. The hire is a match of work, people, and ownership.

## Read the portfolio for the kind of work

Open the work before you open the services list. You are looking for a relative of your project, not for a style you admire in the abstract.

A brand shop that needs to leave an older ecommerce stack should find a migration and a redesign, with the catalog still recognizable. Down the Cove is that kind of public project: ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign. A heritage brand that needs a modern editorial site should find something like Thomas Bewick, where the craft stays legible. A community or a calm brand site has other relatives: Ballarat Box Sports, Wabisabi. An early product interface has others again: Got Next, Leadly, and the scanning-focused Trade Moai concept.

You do not need a studio that has shipped your exact industry. You need evidence they have held a similar constraint. A marketing site and a trading interface are different jobs. Liking the type on one does not mean the team will make good decisions on the other.

Read past the pictures. A useful case names the constraint, the decision, and what changed in the work. Google’s notes on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) ask a question you can turn around on a portfolio: does this show first-hand experience, or could anyone have written it from a screenshot? If the page never says what was hard, you have learned that the studio’s public proof is thin. That is allowed. It is also a reason to ask, on a call, what they would want a visitor to understand.

## Meet the people who will do it

Ask who designs, who builds, and who you will hear from during the project. On a small studio those may be the same few people. That is a feature when you want design and code to stay one idea. It is a warning only if nobody can say who writes production code.

The pitch and the project should be the same team. If a senior person sells the work and an unnamed bench delivers it, you do not yet know the craft you are buying. Ask to meet the person who will be in the files. A short conversation about how they would start is enough. You are not owed a free design.

Listen for how they talk about your buyer. A studio that can restate the offer in a sentence has started the job. A studio that talks only about awards, tools, or a process diagram has not. Hanabi’s public line is specific on purpose: the studio designs and builds websites and product interfaces for founders, with clarity over complexity. You should be able to get a sentence like that from anyone you hire, in their words, about their practice.

Tools are secondary, and they are still fair to ask. A team that designs in Figma and builds in Next.js, React, and TypeScript can show you both. A team that only shows static pictures cannot show you how the page behaves. Ask for one live URL in the portfolio, and open it on your phone.

## Own the result

Ownership is the part founders skip because the pictures are more interesting. Put it in the hiring criteria anyway.

You should leave with the repository, the domain, the analytics property, and the logins for content. Brand files, docs, and project updates should sit somewhere you can open without asking the studio to forward a zip. Hanabi’s client portal is one version of that place. Another studio might use a shared drive. The test is whether you can find the logo, the type, and the latest decision after the invoice is paid.

Code ownership means you can hire someone else later. The stack should be one a competent developer can read. Secrets should be in your accounts, not in a personal login. If the studio’s name is the only admin on the domain, you have rented a website.

Ask what “done” includes. A launch with no way to edit the headline is not done. A launch where every sentence requires a developer might be an honest scope, and it should be said before you sign. Structured fields for the things that change are part of the product, not a favor.

## What a small studio is for

Hire a studio when you need a defined launch and you do not want to assemble the skills yourself. The usual shape is a marketing site, a brand system small enough to use, an ecommerce rebuild, or a focused product interface. The studio is the senior seat for that stretch of work.

Do not hire a studio to be your entire company. Ongoing product decisions, hiring, and support can be a later relationship. They are a different contract from a first site. If the work never stops, an in-house hire may be the better shape. If the task is one skill for a week, a freelancer may be enough. The studio earns its place when design and build have to land together, on a date, as one public thing.

Fit also includes what the studio will refuse. A good partner will say when the project is a template with a logo swap, or when the scope is three products pretending to be one. You want that sentence early. Politeness that hides a mismatch becomes a change request in month two.

## A short list before you book

Use this before you spend a call.

- One project in the portfolio that shares your constraint.
- A live page you can open on a phone.
- The names of the people who will design and build.
- A sentence on what you will own: repo, domain, content, brand files.
- A sense of the edge: what is in the launch, and what is later.

If those are present, a conversation is worth it. If the portfolio is only mood, or ownership is “we’ll see,” keep looking. The cost of a second call is lower than the cost of a rebuild you cannot edit.

Bring the offer in a few sentences, three references, and what must not change. You do not need a forty-page deck. You need enough for the studio to tell you whether they are the right hands.

The questions that go deeper on performance, access, and ownership are gathered in [questions to ask about performance, access, and ownership](/blog/questions-to-ask-a-studio). Use them once the portfolio has already passed.
